elements.texte:
[cheerful] NutriBoost is launching wellness workshops, led by coaches and open to all its customers.

In the previous lesson, you split the information of the Excel file into three tables.

These are the coaches, workshops and enrollments tables.

But the enrollments table only holds the enrollment dates.

No way to know which customer enrolled on September 4, or in which workshop.

To find out, the tables have to be linked with keys.
elements.avant: Link the tables together with primary and foreign keys.
elements.apres: First, each row needs an ID: a value that refers to it alone.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] First, each row needs an ID: a value that refers to it alone.

Your turn!

We add an ID column: each coach gets a unique ID there, which stays the same.

It’s the table’s primary key: each table gets its own.

A primary key can’t be empty (null).

elements.apres: The customers table already had its primary key, ID.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] The customers table already had its primary key, ID.

Next, each enrollment has to be linked to its customer.

We add a customer underscore ID column to the enrollments table: the ID of each row’s customer.

A column that refers to the primary key of another table is a foreign key.

It links each enrollment to its customer: here, customer underscore ID is 1, Sophie Martin’s ID.

Likewise, workshop underscore ID refers to the primary key of the workshops table.

Your turn!

So it’s Léa Simon who enrolled on September 4, in the Healthy cooking workshop.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] One relationship is left to create: each workshop is led by a coach from the coaches table.

Your turn!

Moussa leads two workshops: 2 and 5.

Let’s imagine a workshop underscore ID column in the coaches table.

Both IDs would have to go in the same cell.

Impossible: a cell must hold only one value.

To keep one value per cell, we put coach underscore ID instead in the workshops table.

This way, each workshop shows the coach who leads it.

Your turn!

The Meditation workshop has coach underscore ID equals 4: that’s exactly the ID of Diego Ramos in the coaches table.

A coach can lead several workshops.

Each workshop is led by a single coach.

It’s a “one-to-many” relationship, written 1 to N: the N means “many”.

The rule: in a 1 to N relationship, the foreign key goes on the “many” side.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] Your turn!

To enroll Sophie in the Meditation workshop, we add a row to enrollments.

It holds Sophie’s ID (1), the workshop’s (4) and the enrollment date.

A customer can take part in several workshops.

A workshop can welcome several customers.

It’s a “many-to-many” relationship, written N to N.

An association table records this participation.

Each row holds a customer’s ID and a workshop’s ID.

These two IDs are foreign keys.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] We create a cards table: its foreign key customer underscore ID points to each card’s owner.

A customer has only one card, and a card has only one customer: it’s a “one-to-one” relationship, written 1 to 1.

We add the UNIQUE constraint to the foreign key customer underscore ID.

This way, a customer can appear only once in the cards table.

Since Sophie already has a card, adding a second one is refused.

Your turn!

In a 1 to 1 relationship, a unique foreign key links the two tables.

In a 1 to N relationship, the foreign key goes on the “many” side.

In an N to N relationship, an association table links the two tables, with one row per link.

In the next lesson, you’ll draw this model with a UML diagram.
